newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Scandal, bad news seen pulling down Seoul shares.
newsitem.headline: Scandal, bad news seen pulling down Seoul shares.

text.p: South Korean share prices were seen falling on Thursday in an absence of solid positive news and a continuation of negative factors, including a political scandal involving the president's son, traders and dealers said.
The Korea composite price index closed on Tuesday at 683.86 points, up 11.76 or 1.75 percent. The market was closed on Wednesday for Buddha's Birthday.
Traders said they did not expect Tuesday's rally to last as market fundamentals had not improved.
"Tuesday was just a technical rebound," said D.K. Song, a dealer at H.G. Asia.
"Demand is not good and customer deposits are gradually coming down. I think the index needs a little bit more of a correction," said Song.

Prosecutors said on Wednesday Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, would be summoned for questioning by 2 p.m. (0500 GMT) on Thursday over allegations that he had amassed illicit funds from companies.
"That's always a small bomb waiting to explode," said Chang Ho-sun, equities and derivatives trader at Bankers Trust.
Continuing concerns about the financial health of listed firms were also seen as dragging down stock prices.
Chang said the market would also view a reported delay in implementation of financial reforms as negative news.
A Dainong Group executive has been quoted by domestic media as saying it would sell real estate and unprofitable affiliates to alleviate what he described as a temporary cash flow.
Dainong Corp and Midopa Department Store, the group's key units, have been battered by rumours about liquidity problems at Midopa.
On the positive side, the continuing firming of the yen against the dollar could provide a lift to Korean share prices, as it has all week.

Export-related shares, particularly shipbuilding and automotive stocks, were among the major beneficiaries of the yen. For example, Daewoo Heavy Industries went limit-up on Monday and Tuesday. The yen was trading at 118.91/94 to the dollar late on Wednesday in Tokyo.
"People are definitely saying it's time to move away from domestic cyclical shares to export-related blue chips," said Chang.
"If the yen moves to 116 or 115 against the dollar, we'll see a dramatic change for Korean companies," said Song.
